title: Redundant Connection
problemStatement:
In this problem, a tree is an undirected graph that is connected and has no cycles.

You are given a graph that started as a tree with n nodes labeled from 1 to n, with one additional edge added. The added edge has two different vertices chosen from 1 to n, and was not an edge that already existed. The graph is represented as an array edges of length n where edges[i] = [a, b] indicates that there is an edge between nodes a and b in the graph.

Return an edge that can be removed so that the resulting graph is a tree of n nodes. If there are multiple answers, return the answer that occurs last in the input.

examples.explanation: The edge [2,3] creates a cycle with nodes 1, 2, and 3. Removing it leaves a valid tree.
The edge [1,4] creates a cycle with nodes 1, 2, 3, and 4. Removing it leaves a valid tree.

solutions.detailedExplanation: This brute-force approach simulates the graph construction process by adding edges one at a time. After adding each edge, we run DFS to check if a cycle has formed. The key insight is that a tree with n nodes has exactly n-1 edges, so the nth edge must create a cycle. We build the adjacency list incrementally, and after each edge addition, we create a fresh visited array and run DFS from one endpoint of the newly added edge. If DFS finds a visited node that isn't the parent, we've detected a cycle, meaning the current edge is redundant. The DFS uses parent tracking to handle undirected edges correctly - we skip the edge back to the parent to avoid false cycle detection. This approach guarantees we find the last edge that creates a cycle, as required by the problem. While not optimal due to repeated DFS calls, it's straightforward and correct.
commonMistakes: Not creating a fresh visited array after adding each edge (incorrect cycle detection)
Forgetting to skip parent edges in undirected graph (false cycle detection)
Starting DFS from a random node instead of one endpoint of the new edge (inefficiency)
Not adding edges bidirectionally for undirected graph (incomplete adjacency list)
Returning the first edge instead of continuing to find the last one
solutions.whyItWorks: The algorithm works because a tree is defined as a connected acyclic graph. With n nodes, a tree has exactly n-1 edges. When we add the nth edge, it must create a cycle since all nodes are already connected. By checking for cycles after each edge addition, we detect exactly when the redundant edge is added. The DFS correctly identifies cycles by tracking visited nodes while avoiding false positives from parent edges. Since we process edges in order and return the first edge that creates a cycle, we naturally return the last such edge in the input.
keyInsights: A tree with n nodes has exactly n-1 edges, so the nth edge creates a cycle
Incremental edge addition allows detecting the exact edge that forms the cycle
Parent tracking in DFS is crucial for correct cycle detection in undirected graphs
Fresh visited array after each edge ensures independent cycle checks
Processing edges in order naturally returns the last redundant edge

Add edge [2,3]: adj={1:[2,3], 2:[1,3], 3:[1,2]}, DFS from 2: visit 2, explore 1, from 1 explore 3, from 3 explore 2 (already visited), cycle detected! Return [2,3].

solutions.detailedExplanation: This optimal DFS approach improves upon the naive solution by building the complete graph once and using a single DFS traversal to identify all cycle nodes. The key innovation is tracking the cycle start point and collecting all nodes between the cycle detection and returning to the cycle start. When DFS visits an already-visited node, we've found a cycle and mark that node as cycleStart. As the recursion unwinds, we add each node to the cycle set until we reach cycleStart again, at which point we reset cycleStart to -1 to stop collection. This precisely captures all nodes forming the cycle. After DFS completes, we iterate through edges in reverse order to find the last edge where both endpoints are in the cycle - this is our redundant connection. The algorithm is optimal because it requires only one DFS traversal and one reverse iteration through edges.
commonMistakes: Not resetting cycleStart to -1 after completing cycle (collecting too many nodes)
Forgetting to check if cycleStart is -1 before adding to cycle set (incorrect cycle nodes)
Iterating edges forward instead of reverse (returning wrong edge)
Not using nonlocal keyword in Python for cycleStart (variable scope issue)
Adding cycleStart itself to cycle set before checking equality (off-by-one error)
solutions.whyItWorks: The algorithm works by leveraging DFS's backtracking property to identify cycle nodes. When we detect a cycle (visiting an already-visited node), we know we're at the cycle's starting point. As we unwind the recursive calls, we're traversing back along the path that formed the cycle, so we collect all these nodes. The cycleStart flag ensures we stop collecting once we've completed the full cycle. Since the problem asks for the last edge in the input that's part of the cycle, we reverse-iterate through edges and return the first edge (last in original order) where both endpoints are cycle nodes. This guarantees we return the correct redundant connection.
keyInsights: Single DFS traversal is sufficient to identify all cycle nodes
Backtracking from cycle detection point naturally traces the cycle path
CycleStart flag controls when to start and stop collecting cycle nodes
Reverse iteration through edges finds the last edge in the cycle
O(V+E) time complexity is optimal for this problem

solutions.detailedExplanation: This solution uses a modified topological sort approach to peel away non-cycle nodes, leaving only the cycle. In a tree (acyclic), we can repeatedly remove leaf nodes (degree 1) until all nodes are gone. However, when a cycle exists, the cycle nodes will never reach degree 1 through this process - they'll stabilize at degree 2 (connected to two other nodes in the cycle). We build the adjacency list and track the degree of each node. We initialize a queue with all degree-1 nodes (leaves) and process them: remove each leaf by decrementing its degree and the degrees of its neighbors. When a neighbor's degree becomes 1, it becomes a new leaf and is added to the queue. After this process completes, only cycle nodes remain with degree 2. We then iterate through edges in reverse to find the last edge where both endpoints have degree 2 (or at least non-zero degree, accounting for the final decrements). This edge is the redundant connection.
commonMistakes: Using degree instead of indegree terminology (confusing but functionally equivalent)
Not initializing queue with all degree-1 nodes (incomplete leaf removal)
Checking for degree == 2 for both endpoints without handling edge cases (should check v > 0)
Forgetting to decrement the current node's degree (though not strictly necessary)
Not iterating edges in reverse (returning wrong edge)
solutions.whyItWorks: The algorithm works by exploiting the property that leaf nodes in a tree can be iteratively removed until nothing remains. When a cycle exists, it's impossible to reduce the cycle nodes below degree 2 because each cycle node is connected to exactly two other cycle nodes. The leaf-removal process (topological sort) naturally isolates the cycle by peeling away all non-cycle portions of the graph. After this process, nodes with degree 2 are guaranteed to be part of the cycle. Since we want the last edge in the input that's part of the cycle, we reverse-iterate and return the first edge (last in original order) connecting two cycle nodes.
keyInsights: Leaf removal (topological sort) isolates the cycle from the rest of the graph
Cycle nodes maintain degree 2 after all leaves are removed
BFS-style processing efficiently removes leaves layer by layer
Degree tracking provides cycle membership information without explicit DFS
Reverse iteration ensures we return the last redundant edge

solutions.detailedExplanation: The Union-Find approach is the most efficient solution for this problem. We initialize each node as its own disjoint set (each is its own parent). The find operation locates the representative (root) of a node's set, using path compression to flatten the tree structure for future efficiency. The union operation attempts to merge two sets: if both nodes already belong to the same set (same root), they're already connected, so adding an edge between them creates a cycle - this edge is redundant. If they're in different sets, we merge them using union by rank (attaching the smaller tree to the larger one to maintain balance). We process edges in order, and the first edge that fails to union (returns false) is our answer. This is elegant because it directly models the incremental graph construction: we start with isolated nodes and connect them one edge at a time, detecting the exact moment when we try to add an edge that would create a cycle.
commonMistakes: Not implementing path compression in find (O(n) worst case per operation)
Not implementing union by rank (unbalanced trees, poor performance)
Using size instead of rank for union (works but slightly different semantics)
Forgetting that edges are 1-indexed while par/rank arrays need size n+1
Not processing edges in order (would miss the last redundant edge requirement)
solutions.whyItWorks: Union-Find perfectly models the tree construction process. Initially, n disjoint sets represent n isolated nodes. Each edge should connect two separate components (successful union). When an edge attempts to connect nodes already in the same component, it would create a cycle, violating the tree property. The failed union (p1 == p2) directly detects this condition. Path compression and union by rank optimizations ensure near-constant amortized time per operation (α(n), where α is the inverse Ackermann function). Processing edges in order guarantees we detect the last redundant edge as required by the problem.
keyInsights: Union-Find naturally detects cycle creation in incremental graph construction
Failed union (same root) indicates nodes are already connected via some path
Path compression flattens trees during find for O(α(n)) amortized time
Union by rank maintains balanced trees to prevent degeneration
Most efficient solution with O(E * α(V)) time complexity
No need to store or traverse adjacency list - pure set operations

example1.explanation: Initialize: par=[0,1,2,3], rank=[1,1,1,1]. Process [1,2]: find(1)=1, find(2)=2, different, union succeeds, par=[0,1,1,3], rank=[1,2,1,3]. Process [1,3]: find(1)=1, find(3)=3, different, union succeeds, par=[0,1,1,1], rank=[1,3,1,1]. Process [2,3]: find(2)=1 (path compression), find(3)=1, same root! Union fails, return [2,3].

example2.explanation: Process [1,2]: union succeeds. Process [2,3]: union succeeds. Process [3,4]: union succeeds. Now 1,2,3,4 are in same set. Process [1,4]: find(1) and find(4) return same root, union fails, return [1,4].
